title: Burns: assessment and fluid resuscitation

header.contentArea: Burns emergency: airway, burn size and fluid resuscitation
guidelineVersions: British Burn Association (BBA) & National Burns Network First Aid Statement (7 August 2026)
BBA First Aid Clinical Practice Guideline (24 September 2018)
BBA National Burn Care Referral Guidance (2012)
BBA National Standards for Burn Care (2nd ed., June 2023)
Emergency Management of Severe Burns (EMSB) course manual, UK 19th ed., 2024 (ANZBA course, run in the UK by the BBA)

related.why: both require early escalation and reassessment.
both test perfusion and fluid response, but burn resuscitation has burn-specific formulae and referral criteria.

brief.scenario: You are the core surgical trainee asked to assess an adult transferred to the emergency department after a kitchen fire.
brief.task: Assess immediate threats, interpret the burn information, explain the initial fluid calculation and state your next actions. You have 9 minutes after 1 minute reading time.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Airway and inhalation injury first; then ABCDE, burn size, time-based fluid estimate, temperature control and specialist referral.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Starting with a formula while a hoarse voice may signal evolving airway oedema; treating Parkland as a universal prescription; failing to account for time since injury.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: “I am concerned about evolving inhalation injury. I want senior ED and anaesthetic help now while I assess ABCDE, give high-flow oxygen and prepare for a controlled airway plan.”

flow: Recognise airway threat; call senior ED/anaesthetics and burns service early; give high-flow oxygen 15 L/min via a non-rebreather mask and monitor.
Complete ABCDE, look for enclosed-space exposure, soot, facial/oral burns, voice change, stridor and associated trauma.
Expose safely, stop burning, cool with cool running water for 20 minutes if within 3 hours, avoid hypothermia; estimate partial/full-thickness TBSA.
Use the stated weight, TBSA and elapsed time to calculate a starting fluid estimate; explain the local-protocol variation and titrate to response.
Give titrated IV opioid analgesia, check tetanus status, cover with cling-film strips/layers without circumferential wrapping, document and arrange burns-centre referral/transfer.

grid.label: Airway priority
grid.fail: Ignores hoarseness or delays help while calculating fluid.
grid.borderline: Mentions inhalation injury but does not escalate promptly.
grid.pass: Recognises possible evolving airway injury; calls senior/anaesthetic help and monitors.
grid.high: Explains that oedema can progress and plans early controlled airway management by an experienced team if concern persists.

grid.label: ABCDE and monitoring
grid.fail: No structured assessment; leaves patient unmonitored.
grid.pass: Systematic ABCDE, ECG/BP/SpO₂ monitoring and repeated observations.
grid.high: Delegates tasks, reassesses response and anticipates deterioration.

grid.label: Inhalation / CO risk
grid.fail: Misses enclosed-space exposure, soot or voice change; falsely reassured by SpO₂.
grid.borderline: Names inhalation injury but gives incomplete clues or tests.
grid.pass: Asks about enclosed-space exposure; checks voice, soot, facial/oral burns, stridor and mental state; gives 15 L/min oxygen via non-rebreather; sends blood gas with co-oximetry.
grid.high: Notes normal SpO₂ does not exclude carbon monoxide poisoning; considers cyanide if lactate is high after an enclosed-space fire; seeks senior/toxicology advice.

grid.label: TBSA and depth
grid.fail: Grossly inaccurate estimate or counts simple erythema in resuscitation TBSA.
grid.pass: Uses adult Rule of Nines/palm method appropriately; counts partial/full-thickness burns, records depth uncertainty.
grid.high: Explains Lund–Browder is more precise in children and reassesses burn depth/extent.

grid.label: Fluid estimate
grid.fail: No calculation or presents an unqualified fixed volume as definitive.
grid.borderline: Attempts calculation but ignores elapsed time or local protocol.
grid.pass: Calculates 3 mL × 70 kg × 27 = 5,670 mL/24 h as the EMSB modified Parkland starting estimate; 2,835 mL by 8 h from injury; 45 min elapsed leaves 7 h 15 min, giving about 391 mL/h for the remaining first-8-hour period if no fluid already given.
grid.high: States formulae vary (original Parkland 4 mL/kg/%TBSA, ATLS 2 mL/kg/%TBSA); verifies regional protocol and titrates to perfusion/urine output rather than chasing the formula.

grid.label: Resuscitation endpoints
grid.fail: Does not monitor response or urine output.
grid.borderline: Mentions urine output but no target or reassessment.
grid.pass: Catheterises and uses hourly urine output, perfusion, observations and repeat bloods; adult urine output target approximately 0.5 mL/kg/h (35 mL/h for 70 kg).
grid.high: Adjusts fluid to response and seeks specialist advice if poor response or escalating requirements.

grid.label: First aid, analgesia, warming
grid.fail: Uses ice, delays analgesia or allows hypothermia.
grid.pass: If within 3 h, cool with cool running water for 20 min while preventing hypothermia; titrated IV opioid; cover with strips/layers of cling film, never wrap circumferentially; check tetanus.
grid.high: Explains cooling benefit may remain up to 3 h and prioritises warming non-burned areas.

grid.label: Referral and handover
grid.borderline: Refers late or omits key details.
grid.pass: Early burns-service advice for suspected inhalation injury and adult partial-thickness burns ≥3% TBSA; documents mechanism, time, weight, TBSA, fluid and response.
grid.high: States formal fluid resuscitation is generally considered above 20% TBSA in adults (EMSB 2024), while local networks may vary; gives structured handover.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: He was rescued from a kitchen fire 45 minutes ago. His voice is becoming hoarse. What do you do?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I would calculate the Parkland fluid first and then see if he needs help.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: His respiratory rate is 26, he has soot around his mouth and his SpO₂ is 95% on high-flow oxygen.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: His oxygen saturation is 95%, so I am reassured that his airway is fine.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: The burn map shows the anterior trunk and anterior surfaces of both upper limbs.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I would count the red skin as burn and give the full formula volume without checking the time or urine output.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: What about first aid and referral?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I would wrap cling film tightly around his chest and wait until morning to refer.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I’d introduce myself, confirm his identity from his wristband, explain what I’m doing as I go and check he agrees, then clean my hands and put on gloves and apron.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I am concerned about evolving inhalation injury because he was in an enclosed fire and is becoming hoarse. I would call senior ED and anaesthetic help and contact the burns service now while starting ABCDE, monitoring and high-flow oxygen at 15 L/min via a non-rebreather mask.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I would check soot, facial and oral burns, stridor, work of breathing and mental state. A normal pulse oximeter reading does not exclude carbon monoxide poisoning; I would send an arterial or venous blood gas with co-oximetry for carboxyhaemoglobin.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: The burn map is anterior trunk 18% plus anterior surfaces of both upper limbs 4.5% each.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: That is 27% TBSA, counting partial and full-thickness burns but not simple erythema.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Using the EMSB modified Parkland estimate, 3 mL times 70 kg times 27 gives 5,670 mL over 24 hours. Half is 2,835 mL in the first 8 hours from the time of injury. Forty-five minutes have passed, so if no fluid has been given, that half over the remaining 7 hours 15 minutes is about 391 mL per hour. I would check the regional burn protocol and titrate to response, not treat the formula as fixed.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I would give warmed Hartmann’s solution, insert a urinary catheter and monitor hourly urine output, aiming around 35 mL/hour for 70 kg, reassess perfusion and observations, give titrated IV opioid analgesia, keep him warm, check tetanus, cool the burn for 20 minutes if within 3 hours and safe, then lay cling film in strips without wrapping the chest or limb. I would arrange urgent specialist assessment and document a clear handover.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I’d introduce myself to him and the team, confirm his identity from his wristband, explain each step as I go so he can agree to it, and clean my hands and put on gloves and apron before touching him.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I will delegate monitoring, access, bloods and warming while remaining responsible for the airway decision; progressive hoarseness after enclosed-space exposure needs immediate senior/anaesthetic review.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I would not use a reassuring SpO₂ to exclude carbon monoxide exposure. Alongside high-flow oxygen and co-oximetry, I would check lactate: a high lactate after an enclosed-space fire makes me consider cyanide toxicity and seek senior/toxicology advice, while avoiding delay to airway management.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The TBSA is 27%: 18% anterior trunk plus 4.5% for each anterior upper limb. The estimate is uncertain until the burn is fully assessed, and erythema alone is excluded.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Modified Parkland gives 5,670 mL/24 h and 2,835 mL by hour 8 after injury; with 45 minutes elapsed, the illustrative rate is about 391 mL/hour only if no fluid has already been administered. This is a starting estimate, not a target to chase. Other formulae use 2 or 4 mL/kg/%TBSA, so I will follow the receiving burn network’s protocol and titrate to physiology.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I would use a balanced crystalloid such as Hartmann’s and insert a urinary catheter; for 70 kg, the hourly urine output target is about 35 mL. I will track perfusion, lactate/renal function and urine output, and call the burn team if response or fluid requirements are concerning.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I would check for circumferential chest burns restricting excursion; if constricting eschar impaired ventilation, I would urgently involve the burn, anaesthetic and surgical teams for escharotomy consideration. I would cool for 20 minutes with cool running water if within 3 hours, warm the rest of the patient, use titrated IV opioid, check tetanus, apply cling film as loose strips and arrange urgent referral to a burns centre, because 27% TBSA with suspected inhalation injury meets the EMSB burns-centre threshold (25% or more with inhalation injury); formal fluid resuscitation is generally considered above 20% TBSA in adults, subject to network protocol, then give a structured handover.

failures.move: Delays senior/anaesthetic airway review despite progressive hoarseness after an enclosed fire.
failures.consequence: Airway oedema may progress to obstruction before a controlled airway is secured.

failures.move: Uses normal SpO₂ to dismiss possible carbon monoxide poisoning/inhalation injury.
failures.consequence: Hypoxia or toxic exposure may be missed and treatment delayed.

failures.move: Administers a fixed fluid volume without accounting for elapsed time or reassessing response.
failures.consequence: Under- or over-resuscitation may cause shock or fluid-related harm.

failures.move: Wraps cling film circumferentially or delays urgent burns referral.
failures.consequence: Constriction/thermal risk and delay to specialist airway and burn care.

recovery.when: If you did not prioritise the airway threat first
recovery.line: I need to prioritise the airway threat first; I can calculate fluid while the senior airway and burns teams are being called.

recovery.when: If you treated the formula as more than a starting estimate
recovery.line: This formula is a starting estimate only; I will account for time since injury and titrate to physiology under the regional burn protocol.

knowledge.fact: Suspected CO or smoke inhalation: high-flow oxygen 15 L/min via a non-rebreather mask; a normal SpO₂ does not exclude CO poisoning; send an arterial or venous blood gas with co-oximetry (carboxyhaemoglobin); in enclosed-space fires with a high lactate, consider cyanide.
In adults, Rule of Nines is a rapid estimate; anterior trunk is 18% and each entire upper limb 9%, with anterior surface about 4.5%. Count partial/full-thickness burns, not simple erythema.

EMSB modified Parkland starting estimate: 3 mL × kg × %TBSA over 24 hours; half in first 8 hours from injury. For 70 kg and 27%: 5,670 mL/24 h; 2,835 mL by hour 8. It is a starting estimate, not a fixed prescription.
Other formulae exist (original Parkland 4 mL/kg/%TBSA; ATLS 2 mL/kg/%TBSA); use the receiving network protocol and titrate to response.

Use a balanced crystalloid such as Hartmann’s; a urinary catheter is needed for hourly urine output. Adult urine output target commonly around 0.5 mL/kg/h; for 70 kg approximately 35 mL/h. Use alongside perfusion, observations and laboratory trends.
Cool with cool running water for 20 minutes, effective up to 3 hours after injury; avoid ice and hypothermia. Lay cling film over the burn in strips; do not wrap circumferentially.

Seek specialist burns advice for suspected inhalation injury; BBA referral guidance identifies adult partial-thickness burns ≥3% TBSA for referral consideration. Formal fluid resuscitation is generally considered above 20% TBSA in adults (10% in children), subject to network protocol.

recall.think: Airway first; burn size; time since injury; protocol-led fluid; reassess.
recall.say: “Possible inhalation injury: I’m escalating airway support now.”
do: ABCDE, 15 L/min oxygen/monitoring, TBSA, time-based calculation, analgesia, warming and referral.

numbers.meaning: Modified Parkland 3 mL/kg/%TBSA, half in first 8 h from burn: 27% → 5,670 mL/24 h, ≈391 mL/h for the remaining 7 h 15 min

recall.trap: Do not calculate first while the airway deteriorates.
recall.finish: Reassess airway, perfusion and urine output; document handover.

partner.opening: He was pulled from a kitchen fire about 45 minutes ago. His voice seems rougher and he is increasingly anxious.

reveals.finding: flame in a small enclosed kitchen; inside for about 5 minutes before rescue.
sore throat and hoarse voice developing over 20 minutes; no reported loss of consciousness.
RR 26/min, SpO₂ 95% on high-flow oxygen, HR 122/min, BP 104/68 mmHg, temperature 36.0°C, GCS 15.

reveals.trigger: Reveal only if asked: Weight and burn map
reveals.finding: Weight 70 kg. Burn map: anterior trunk 18%; anterior surface of each upper limb 4.5%; total 27% TBSA. No fluid has been administered yet.
No circumferential chest burn is shown; if asked, examiner says chest excursion is currently adequate but must be reassessed.

push.question: If candidate delays: “His voice sounds worse and he is becoming more agitated.”

curveballs.prompt: “His SpO₂ is 98% now. Does that rule out carbon monoxide poisoning or evolving airway injury?”
curveballs.safeAnswer: no; assess exposure and airway, continue 15 L/min oxygen via a non-rebreather mask, send a blood gas with co-oximetry, and do not delay airway escalation.

curveballs.prompt: “Can I wrap cling film all the way around his chest?”
curveballs.safeAnswer: no; lay strips/layers over the burn, never circumferentially.

curveballs.prompt: “His full-thickness chest burn is circumferential and chest excursion is restricted.”
curveballs.safeAnswer: urgent senior burn/anaesthetic/surgical review; escharotomy may be required if constricting eschar compromises ventilation.
